description: Discovery advertisement vectors. The canonical TXT payload and the beacon canonicalisation are pinned so that the signature a controller verifies is unambiguous. See RFC-0003 sections 2 and 4.1.

txt_canonicalisation.rule: Keys appear in exactly this order, separated by 0x0A, with the label and a NUL first. No trailing newline.
txt_canonicalisation.note: The order is fixed rather than alphabetical so that a reader can compare the specification, the vector and the code without consulting a sort implementation. The optional keys (model, android, sdk, busy, loc, tls) are covered by 'sig_extra_keys' below: they are appended after 'port' in the order listed in RFC-0003 section 2 when present.

vectors.note: The smallest legal advertisement: the five required keys only.

An advertisement with every optional key, in the fixed extra-key order. A controller that can verify the signature must accept it; one that cannot must treat the device as unverified rather than ignoring it.
vectors.canonical_utf8:
DLWP/1-txt�v=1.0
id=aaaaaaaa-bbbb-4ccc-8ddd-eeeeeeeeeeee
fp=DE34-A1B0-77C9-9021
caps=screen.mirror,input.touch,input.key,shell.exec,adb.wireless
port=45917
model=Pixel 7
android=14
sdk=34
busy=0
loc=lan
tls=0
vectors.canonical_length_note: 208 UTF-8 bytes. Measured, not estimated: the optional keys add 87 bytes over discovery.txt.minimal's 121.

vectors.note: When the capability list would push the record past the size budget the agent truncates it and sets a trailing comma-free prefix. A controller must treat the list as advisory and call GET_CAPABILITIES after connecting, because a truncated list is not evidence that a capability is missing.
vectors.note_on_trust: The advertised list is a hint. Only the CAPABILITIES frame after authentication is authoritative.

vectors.note: The beacon fields are canonicalised in ascending key order with no whitespace, and every field except sig is covered by the signature. This differs from the TXT canonicalisation on purpose: the beacon carries a JSON object, so it uses its own deterministic rule.

rejection_vectors.note: A controller that holds a pairing record for the advertised id verifies the signature. A mismatch means the advertisement is forged, which is a real attack: an attacker on the LAN trying to redirect the controller to their own listener.
rejection_vectors.note_on_action: The controller must not connect. It must also not quietly remove the device: an attacker may be jamming the real agent, so the UI keeps the device listed as unverified and offers a manual connect.

rejection_vectors.note: The id matches a pairing record but the fingerprint does not. This is the identity-change case that RFC-0003 section 3.2 treats as a possible impersonation.
A record set larger than the mDNS budget cannot be delivered reliably in one response, so the agent must not produce it.
The beacon is a broadcast; it must not be emitted when the operator has disabled discovery, and the agent must not unicast it to an address it has not itself been contacted from.

lifecycle_vectors.note: Turning discovery off sends a goodbye with TTL 0 so controllers drop the device promptly instead of waiting out the record TTL.
A Wi-Fi roam or DHCP renewal changes the address, and the advertisement must carry the new one. This is the most common cause of a device appearing online but being unreachable.
Presence expires after the TTL, but the pairing survives. An offline device stays in the saved list so the user can see it and reconnect later.
An agent at its session limit keeps advertising with busy=1, so a controller can show a reason rather than 'device not found'.
